common_name: Fragrant Cloud Rose (Intensely Fragrant Coral-Red Hybrid Tea)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container roses in late winter or early spring in slightly acidic, well-amended, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Fragrant Cloud is a German-bred 1960s hybrid tea celebrated as one of the most fragrant roses ever introduced.

directions: Plant in slightly acidic, well-amended, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Fragrant Cloud produces large, high-centered, coral-red double blooms carrying one of the strongest, most widely admired fragrances of any hybrid tea rose, a heavy old-rose scent that has made it a benchmark for rose perfume since its introduction. Its flower color deepens with age and cooler weather, and the strong scent carries well beyond the immediate area of the plant, making it a favorite for cutting gardens sited near patios or windows. As with most classic hybrid teas, expect to manage black spot and powdery mildew with a regular preventative spray program in humid, rainy climates. Prune hard in late winter, feed monthly through the growing season, and deadhead spent blooms to encourage repeat flowering.
sources: World Federation of Rose Societies — Rose Hall of Fame

common_name: Perfume Delight Rose (Fragrant Deep Pink Hybrid Tea)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container roses in late winter or early spring in slightly acidic, well-amended, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Perfume Delight is an AARS-winning 1970s hybrid tea grown as much for its heavy old-rose fragrance as for its flower form.

directions: Plant in slightly acidic, well-amended, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Perfume Delight bears large, high-centered, deep pink double flowers with a strong, classic old-rose fragrance that was central to its All-America Rose Selections win, at a time when many newer hybrid teas were being bred with less attention to scent. Its vigorous, upright growth and reliable repeat bloom made it a long-standing favorite for cutting gardens where fragrance is a priority. As with most classic hybrid teas, a regular preventative spray program helps manage black spot and powdery mildew in humid climates. Prune hard in late winter, feed monthly through the growing season, and deadhead spent blooms to sustain the bloom cycle.
sources: World Federation of Rose Societies — Rose Hall of Fame

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container roses in late winter or early spring in slightly acidic, well-amended, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Sunsprite is a German-bred floribunda long valued for combining strong fragrance with a clear, non-fading yellow flower color.

directions: Plant in slightly acidic, well-amended, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Sunsprite bears clusters of bright, clear golden-yellow double flowers with a notably strong, sweet fragrance, unusual for a yellow rose, since many yellow cultivars carry little to no scent. Its compact, bushy floribunda habit produces flowers in generous clusters rather than one bloom per stem, giving a fuller, more continuous show through the growing season than many hybrid teas. It shows better disease resistance than many older yellow roses but still benefits from a preventative fungicide program in humid, rainy climates. Deadhead spent clusters to encourage continued rebloom, and prune moderately in late winter to shape the plant.
sources: World Federation of Rose Societies — Rose Hall of Fame

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container roses in late winter or early spring in slightly acidic, well-amended, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Angel Face is an AARS 1969 winner grown for its unusual lavender-mauve color and strong fragrance.

directions: Plant in slightly acidic, well-amended, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Angel Face bears ruffled, lavender-mauve double flowers with a strong, spicy-sweet fragrance, an All-America Rose Selections winner notable for a flower color rarely seen in floribundas of its era. Its compact, bushy habit produces flowers in clusters through a long summer bloom season, and the distinctive color pairs well with pink and white companions in a mixed rose bed. As with many older rose cultivars, a preventative fungicide program helps manage black spot and powdery mildew in humid, rainy climates. Deadhead spent clusters to encourage continued rebloom, and prune moderately in late winter to maintain a full, well-shaped plant.
sources: World Federation of Rose Societies — Rose Hall of Fame

common_name: Sterling Silver Rose (Historic Lavender Hybrid Tea)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container roses in late winter or early spring in slightly acidic, well-amended, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Sterling Silver, introduced in the 1950s, was one of the first commercially successful lavender roses and remains valued for its color and fragrance despite modest vigor and disease resistance by modern standards.

directions: Plant in slightly acidic, well-amended, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Sterling Silver was one of the earliest widely grown lavender hybrid tea roses, its soft silvery-lavender double flowers carrying a strong, sweet fragrance that helped popularize lavender as a serious rose color when it was introduced in the 1950s. It tends toward more modest vigor and disease resistance than later lavender rose introductions, so a consistent feeding program and a preventative fungicide schedule for black spot and powdery mildew are especially important in humid, rainy climates. Deadhead spent blooms to encourage repeat flowering, and prune hard in late winter to keep the plant vigorous and productive.
sources: World Federation of Rose Societies — Rose Hall of Fame

common_name: Oklahoma Rose (Near-Black Deep Red Fragrant Hybrid Tea)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container roses in late winter or early spring in slightly acidic, well-amended, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Oklahoma is a 1960s hybrid tea grown for its extremely dark, near-black red flower color and strong fragrance.

directions: Plant in slightly acidic, well-amended, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Oklahoma bears large, velvety, near-black deep red double blooms with a strong, classic old-rose fragrance, among the darkest flower colors available in the genus at the time of its introduction. The intensely dark petals can be prone to sunburn and browning in the hottest, most intense afternoon sun, so a site with some relief from the harshest midday exposure helps preserve flower quality. As with most classic hybrid teas, a regular preventative fungicide program helps manage black spot and powdery mildew in humid, rainy climates. Prune hard in late winter, feed monthly through the growing season, and deadhead spent blooms to sustain repeat flowering.
sources: World Federation of Rose Societies — Rose Hall of Fame
